```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

Use `variance_comp()` to answer two questions. How strongly does the model
penalise its smooth and random-effect coefficients? How much do the fitted
contributions of its terms vary across the observations? The first is about
the model's coefficients. The second also depends on the observed covariate
values. A linear term, for example, varies more across observations that
cover a wider range of its covariate, even with the same coefficient.

Load {gratia} and {mgcv}, then simulate 360 observations in 12 groups of 30.
We generate `z` from `x` plus noise so the two are positively correlated. We
generate `w` independently for the nonlinear effect.

```{r covariates}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()

set.seed(2026)
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(360, -1, 1), w = runif(360),
  group = factor(rep(seq_len(12), each = 30)))
dat$z <- 0.8 * dat$x + rnorm(360, sd = 0.2)
```

The response combines positive linear effects of `x` and `z` with a sine wave
in `w`. Add a Gaussian random intercept with standard deviation 0.6, shared by
all observations in the same group, and independent Gaussian noise with
standard deviation 0.4 for each observation. The two linear effects tend to
increase together, so their covariance increases the variance of their sum.

```{r response}
group_effect <- rnorm(12, sd = 0.6)
dat$y <- 2 * dat$x + 1.5 * dat$z + sin(2 * pi * dat$w) +
  group_effect[dat$group] + rnorm(360, sd = 0.4)
```

Fit a model with unpenalised linear terms for `x` and `z`, a smooth for `w`
and a random intercept for `group`.

```{r model}
model <- gam(y ~ x + z + s(w, k = 8) + s(group, bs = "re"),
  data = dat, method = "REML")
```

## Extract penalty variances and variances of fitted terms

First extract the penalty variances, which describe shrinkage of the
penalised coefficients. The `.lower_ci` and `.upper_ci` columns give interval
limits on the standard deviation scale.

```{r penalties}
vc_penalty <- variance_comp(model, type = "penalty")
vc_penalty
```

A penalty variance is the model scale $\phi$ divided by the smoothing
parameter $\lambda_j$. By default, the function expresses $\lambda_j$ on the
scale of the original penalty matrix, undoing the rescaling mgcv applies
during fitting. For a given penalty, a larger variance corresponds to less
shrinkage. There is one row per penalty, so a smooth can have several rows.
For this Gaussian model the `scale` row gives the estimated residual variance.
The unpenalised terms `x` and `z` appear in the fitted term table below.

With `type = "terms"`, we measure how much each term's fitted contribution
varies across the observations used to fit the model. We use 1,000 draws of
the coefficients to calculate intervals and set a seed to make the draws
reproducible.

```{r terms}
vc_terms <- variance_comp(model, type = "terms", n_draws = 1000, seed = 42)
vc_terms
```

These are sample variances on the linear predictor scale, with each
observation counted equally. The output includes unpenalised terms and has
one row for each smooth, even if it has several penalties. Intercepts, offsets
and residual variation are excluded from the calculation.

## Account for covariance when comparing terms

The variance of the sum depends on both the term variances and their
covariances. Let $f_j$ be term $j$'s fitted values, $F = \sum_j f_j$ their sum,
and $C$ their covariance matrix. Then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(F) = \sum_j C_{jj} + 2\sum_{j<k} C_{jk}.
$$

The result stores the covariance matrix of the fitted contributions across
observations. Summing its diagonal gives the sum of the term variances.
Summing all entries also accounts for covariance, so it gives the total
variance of the combined contributions.

```{r covariance}
C <- attr(vc_terms, "covariance")
c(sum_of_term_variances = sum(diag(C)),
  total_including_covariance = sum(C))
```

To divide the total among terms, we split each covariance contribution,
$2C_{jk}$, equally between the two terms. Each term receives its own variance
plus its covariance with every other term, expressed as the proportion
$p_j = \operatorname{Cov}(f_j, F) / \operatorname{Var}(F)$. When the total
variance is positive, the proportions sum to one. Check this by computing only
the individual proportions with `include_total = FALSE` and skipping interval
calculation with `n_draws = 0`.

```{r allocation}
vc_no_total <- variance_comp(model, type = "terms", include_total = FALSE,
  n_draws = 0)
sum(vc_no_total$.proportion)
```

Intervals for the penalty variances account for uncertainty in the estimated
smoothing parameters and model scale. For intervals on the fitted term
variances, we draw all coefficients together from their approximate Gaussian
posterior distribution. We recompute the fitted contributions and their
variances and proportions for each draw. The smoothing parameters stay fixed
at their estimates by default. Use `unconditional = TRUE` to include a
correction for uncertainty in smoothing parameter estimates when the fitted
model supports it. The proportions from each draw are in
`attr(vc_terms, "proportion_draws")$total`. The interval limits describe each
term separately, so the limits need not sum to one.

## Plot term variances and their proportions

Use {patchwork} to show the variances, including the total, alongside the
proportions for the individual terms. Both plots show intervals, with terms
on the x-axis.

```{r plots}
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  draw(vc_terms),
  draw(vc_terms, type = "proportion", include_total = FALSE),
  ncol = 2
)
```

Use `draw(vc_penalty)` for penalty variances or `draw(vc_terms, type = "std_dev")`
for term standard deviations. `draw()` uses the stored intervals, squaring
standard deviation limits when plotting variances.
Use `n_dodge = 2` to stagger term labels, `angle = 45` to rotate them, or
`flip = TRUE` to put terms on the y-axis.

### Why a term's proportion can be negative

To show how a proportion can be negative, we reuse the correlated `x` and `z`
but give their effects opposite signs. The new response combines `2 * x - z`
with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.1, so the two effects partly
cancel each other.

```{r opposing-data}
set.seed(208)
dat$contrast <- 2 * dat$x - dat$z + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = 0.1)
```

Fit both linear terms and plot their proportions with intervals, omitting
the total row.

```{r opposing-terms}
opposing <- gam(contrast ~ x + z, data = dat, method = "REML")
vc_opposing <- variance_comp(opposing, type = "terms", n_draws = 1000, seed = 43)
draw(vc_opposing, type = "proportion", include_total = FALSE)
```

Their negative covariance reduces the variance of their sum. Accounting for
this covariance gives `x` a share of
`r round(vc_opposing$.proportion[vc_opposing$.component == "x"], 2)` and `z` a share of
`r round(vc_opposing$.proportion[vc_opposing$.component == "z"], 2)`.
In this example `z` gets a negative proportion because its covariance with
the contribution of `x` is more negative than its own variance is positive.
The proportions still sum to one, so `x` gets a proportion greater than one.
When the total variance is zero, the proportions are undefined (`NA`).
